name: Diamond Sierra Site Defense
author: teoleonard

sections.description:
Diamond Sierra Site Defense checks your site once a day and tells you – in plain English – what is wrong and how to fix it. Everything below is free, with no account to sign up for, and no firewall rules held back for paying users.

Daily malware scan

  • Compares every WordPress core file against the official checksums from WordPress.org.
  • Compares plugins and themes from the WordPress.org directory against their official copies, so tampered files (supply-chain attacks) are caught and verified files are skipped.
  • Signature scan of themes, plugins, must-use plugins and uploads for web shells, obfuscated eval() backdoors, droppers, hidden-admin code and more.
  • Detects ClickFix / fake CAPTCHA pages that trick visitors into running commands on their own computer, clipboard hijacking scripts, and EtherHiding loaders that pull code from BSC/Polygon smart contracts.
  • Detects injected remote import() calls in files and on the live homepage.
  • Fetches your homepage like a visitor coming from Google, and again as Googlebot, to catch injections and SEO spam that hide from logged-in users.
  • Tracks new and changed PHP files between scans.
  • Risky plugin alerts with no setup and no API key: plugins removed from WordPress.org for a security issue, security updates waiting (found in the plugin’s changelog) and plugins abandoned for over two years.
  • Optional: checks whether Google Safe Browsing is warning visitors away from the site (off until you turn it on).
  • Runs in small steps, so it works on shared hosting without timeouts.

Fixes

  • Restore a modified core, plugin or theme file with the verified original from WordPress.org.
  • Quarantine suspicious files – restorable from the Quarantine tab.
  • A verification scan runs automatically after a fix to confirm the malware is really gone.

Firewall

  • Blocks SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, remote file inclusion, command injection and PHP object injection.
  • Blocks executable and disguised PHP uploads and SVGs with embedded scripts.
  • Blocks vulnerability scanners and probes for .env, .git, wp-config backups and known shell names.
  • Inspects JSON sent to the REST API and cookies, not just forms.
  • Repeat offenders are blocked automatically.
  • Fake search engines: bots pretending to be Googlebot, Bingbot, Applebot, YandexBot or Baiduspider are checked against the real search engine’s network (the IP lists Google, Bing and Apple publish, then reverse and forward DNS) and blocked. Real crawlers and your SEO are not affected.
  • Rate limiting: separate limits a minute for browsers and for bots, either slowing the visitor down (503 with Retry-After) or blocking them. Logged-in users, verified search engines, AJAX and the WooCommerce cart and checkout are never counted.
  • Bad bots: site copiers, email harvesters and scraping frameworks, and form posts with no browser headers, are turned away. SEO tool crawlers (Ahrefs, Semrush and others) can be turned away too.
  • Your own block list: IP addresses and ranges (IPv4 and IPv6), user agents, referring sites and visitor hostnames. A save can never block the admin making it.
  • Comment spam bots are caught with an invisible decoy field and a time stamp, and go to the Spam folder. An IP caught three times in a day is blocked.
  • REST API lock (optional): logged-out visitors can only use the routes front-end features need.
  • 404 probing: an IP hunting for vulnerable plugins and old backups through dozens of missing pages is blocked. Missing images and styles don’t count, and real search engines are never counted.
  • AI training crawlers (optional): GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider and others are told in robots.txt and turned away if they ignore it, while AI assistants fetching a page for a user still get in. The Firewall tab shows which AI bots visit and how often.
  • Log-only mode: see what would be blocked before anything is. New installs log for their first week, then start blocking on their own.

Login protection

  • Two-factor login with any authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Authy…) or with codes sent by email, plus one-time backup codes. Email codes are only turned on after a test code has arrived, so a mailbox that never gets the mail can’t lock anyone out.
  • CAPTCHA on the login, registration, lost-password and comment forms: a built-in math question (no account needed), Cloudflare Turnstile, Google reCAPTCHA v2 or hCaptcha – with step-by-step instructions for getting the keys. A CAPTCHA outage or a wrong key never locks you out.
  • Refuses passwords found in known data breaches (Have I Been Pwned, k-anonymity – the password never leaves your site).
  • Custom login URL – move the login page off wp-login.php so bots can’t find it.
  • Login form honeypot that blocks automated login bots with nothing for real visitors to solve.
  • Limits failed logins per IP and per account, with escalating lockouts. IPs an account has used before are never locked out, so nobody can lock you out of your own site.
  • Trap usernames (like “admin”) get bots locked out on the first try, and can’t be registered as new accounts.
  • Strong passwords for administrators, editors and shop managers, checked on the server wherever a password is set.
  • Login allowlist (optional): powerful accounts can only log in from the IPs you list, while customers log in as before.
  • Generic error messages that don’t reveal whether a username exists.

Email alerts

By default you get one security email a week, on Monday morning, and only when something is new. You can switch to a daily email or to emails straight after every scan.

  • Scans found something serious (and, if you like, an all-clear when nothing is new).
  • An administrator signed in from a new IP (skipped while Wordfence already emails every admin login).
  • A new administrator account was created, or someone was promoted to administrator.
  • Diamond Sierra Site Defense itself was deactivated – malware often switches security plugins off first.
  • Plugin, theme and WordPress updates are waiting (only when a new one appears).
  • How many IPs and accounts were locked out after failed logins (optional).

A new administrator and Site Defense being switched off are always emailed straight away.

Hardening

  • Disable XML-RPC, the file editor, application passwords and username enumeration.
  • Block PHP execution in uploads, sensitive files and directory listing.
  • Security headers and hidden version numbers.
  • A security score that explains every check, each with its own Apply button.

Also

  • Works alongside Wordfence, All-In-One Security, Solid Security, Sucuri, MalCare, Defender, Shield, Loginizer and others: Site Defense pauses its own firewall and login limits so the same visitor isn’t blocked twice, and keeps scanning.
  • Multisite: network-activate it to protect every site. The scanner and settings are for super admins only.
  • Results in Tools → Site Health, and WP-CLI commands to get back in after a lockout (wp site-defense unblock, reset-login-url, 2fa-reset).

Diamond Sierra Site Defense Pro

An optional add-on for people who clean hacked sites or look after many: one-click database cleanup, “Fix automatically”, the post-hack recovery kit, protection against stolen login cookies, supply-chain watches, WooCommerce card-testing and checkout protection, CVE matching, an alert centre with Slack/Discord, an activity log and white-labelling. Everything listed above stays free. Details at diamondsierra.com

External services

Diamond Sierra Site Defense connects to these services. Apart from the WordPress.org checks, each one is off until you turn it on.

  • WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org, downloads.wordpress.org, core.svn.wordpress.org, plugins.svn.wordpress.org, themes.svn.wordpress.org) – to download official checksums, theme packages and clean copies of files when you restore or repair them, and to read the public directory entry of each installed plugin (whether it was closed, when it was last updated, and the changelog of a waiting update). Only the names and versions of WordPress, your plugins and your themes are sent – the same information WordPress itself sends when it checks for updates. Terms
  • Have I Been Pwned – Pwned Passwords (api.pwnedpasswords.com) – only if you turn on “Block breached passwords”. When a password is set, and once a day at login, the first 5 characters of the password’s SHA-1 hash are sent; the password itself and the rest of the hash never leave your site. Terms and privacy
  • Cloudflare Turnstile (challenges.cloudflare.com) – only if you choose Turnstile as the CAPTCHA. Its script is loaded on the protected forms, and on submit the visitor’s token and IP address are sent to Cloudflare to check them. Terms · Privacy
  • Google reCAPTCHA (www.google.com/recaptcha) – only if you choose reCAPTCHA as the CAPTCHA. Its script is loaded on the protected forms, and on submit the visitor’s token and IP address are sent to Google to check them. Terms · Privacy
  • hCaptcha (js.hcaptcha.com, api.hcaptcha.com) – only if you choose hCaptcha as the CAPTCHA. Its script is loaded on the protected forms, and on submit the visitor’s token and IP address are sent to hCaptcha to check them. Terms · Privacy
  • Google Safe Browsing – only if you turn on the blocklist check under Settings → Malware scanner. Once per scan, your site’s address is sent to Google to find out whether it is blocklisted. With an API key the request goes to safebrowsing.googleapis.com; without a key, and only if you also tick “Check without a key”, it goes to transparencyreport.google.com. Nothing else is sent. Terms · Privacy

Privacy

  • Everything Site Defense records stays in your own database. Nothing is sent to us. The only outside connections are the ones listed under External services.
  • The firewall and login logs store the visitor’s IP address, the address they requested and their browser’s user agent, so you can see who was blocked and why. Log lines are deleted after 30 days, and the log never grows past 20,000 lines.
  • Blocked IPs are kept until their block ends.
  • For each user it keeps the last 10 IP addresses they logged in from (so nobody is locked out of their own account and new-IP alerts work), and, if they turn on two-factor login, the authenticator secret and hashed backup codes.
  • The plugin sets no cookies of its own.
  • Only administrators (super admins on multisite) can see the logs and settings.
  • Deleting the plugin removes its tables, settings, user data and quarantined files.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the plugin folder to /wp-content/plugins/ or install the zip from Plugins → Add New.
  2. Activate it.
  3. Go to Site Defense → Dashboard and click Scan now to build the first baseline.
  4. If your site is behind Cloudflare, set Settings → Visitor IP comes from to Cloudflare.

The daily scan uses WP-Cron. On low-traffic sites, a real cron job calling wp-cron.php every 5 minutes makes sure it always runs on time.
sections.faq:
Do I need a Google API key for the blocklist check?

The blocklist check is off by default. To use it, turn on Settings → Malware scanner → Google blocklist check and either paste a free Safe Browsing API key from Google Cloud (recommended, it’s Google’s official API) or tick Check without a key to read the public status from Google’s Transparency Report instead.

My site is behind a load balancer. Which IP setting do I use?

Pick X-Forwarded-For. Site Defense reads that header from the right and takes the first public address, so a visitor can’t fake their IP by sending the header themselves. Behind Cloudflare, pick Cloudflare instead.

I use nginx – is the uploads protection active?

nginx ignores .htaccess files. Add this to your server block:

location ~* /wp-content/uploads/.*\.php$ { deny all; }

A finding is a false positive. What do I do?

Click Ignore. It stays hidden until that file or content changes.

Can I use it with Wordfence or All-In-One Security?

Yes. Run only one firewall – by default Site Defense steps aside and lets the other plugin handle the firewall and login limits, while it keeps scanning and cleaning. If you’d rather use Site Defense’s firewall, switch the other plugin’s firewall off and untick “Step aside for other security plugins” in Settings.

I use Jetpack / the mobile app

Untick Disable XML-RPC in Settings.

I locked myself out by the firewall

With WP-CLI: wp site-defense unblock <your-ip>. Without it, add define( 'DSSD_DISABLE_FIREWALL', true ); to wp-config.php, log in, add your IP under Settings → Never block these IPs, then remove the line again.

I lost my phone and can’t get past two-factor login

Type one of your backup codes instead of the 6-digit code. No backup codes? Ask another administrator to click Turn off under Two-factor login on your user profile, run wp site-defense 2fa-reset <your-user>, or add define( 'DSSD_DISABLE_2FA', true ); to wp-config.php, log in, set it up again, then remove the line.

Why does the firewall say “Would block (log only)”?

New installs spend their first week in log-only mode so you can spot false alarms – a contact form or plugin that legitimately sends code-like text. Check the Firewall tab, then click Start blocking now, or wait and it starts on its own.

I set a custom login URL and can’t find it

Add define( 'DSSD_DISABLE_LOGIN_URL', true ); to wp-config.php. wp-login.php works normally again straight away. Log in, check or clear the URL under Settings → Login protection, then remove the line.

Does the custom login URL work on multisite?

No. On a network, renaming the login page would break sign-on across sites, so the feature turns itself off there automatically.

Does Site Defense work on multisite?

Yes – network-activate it. The firewall, login protection, two-factor login, Turnstile and the activity log protect every site. The scanner, cleanup tools and settings live in the main site’s dashboard and are for super admins only, because they work on files shared by the whole network. Settings apply to all sites.

Can I extend it?

Yes. Filters and actions include dssd_signatures, dssd_firewall_rules, dssd_scan_recurrence, dssd_settings_defaults, dssd_settings_sanitize, dssd_settings_cards, dssd_admin_tabs, dssd_render_tab_{tab}, dssd_brand_name, dssd_menu_label, dssd_show_branding, dssd_import_allowlist, dssd_allow_xmlrpc and dssd_loaded.
sections.changelog:
1.2.0

Lessons from cleaning a WooCommerce shop with malware that kept reinstalling itself.

  • New: accounts are checked for what they can do, not what their role is called. A “customer” with administrator powers is reported as critical, and so are administrators with the machine-made names known malware uses.
  • New: plugins that aren’t on WordPress.org are listed, and reported as critical when they also show signs of malware (obfuscated code, creating administrators, hiding from the Plugins screen, a “security helper” from an unknown personal domain, or a known fake plugin name).
  • New: detection for malware that reinstalls itself: code that turns a plugin back on when you turn it off, restores itself from a zip or a private GitHub repository, or drops must-use plugins. Known watchdog file names and folders are reported too, including renamed copies of the plugins folder.
  • New: the settings and scheduled tasks such malware keeps in the database are reported, so they can be removed together with the files.
  • New: hostile .htaccess files are reported: a root file that blocks PHP but lets the attacker’s own files run, a wp-admin file that locks you out of the dashboard, mixed-case “php” tricks and uploads rules that let PHP run.
  • New: disguised scripts built from meaningless sums, the way card skimmers hide, and links hidden from visitors with screen-reader-text.
  • Fixed: the custom login URL showed “Active” even when wp-config.php turned it off. Settings and Hardening now say so and show the line to remove.
  • Fixed: after saving a login URL, Site Defense now asks the site for it the way a visitor would, and tells you if the server doesn’t serve it. It checks again every day.
  • Fixed: the login URL text box was squeezed by the status line next to it.
  • Fixed: “Block PHP execution in uploads” said it was active when the file couldn’t be written. It now tries to make the file writable, says why it couldn’t (permissions and owner), tests the rule with a harmless file, and tells you when the server doesn’t enforce it.
  • Fixed: when one protection couldn’t be written, the others in the same save were marked as on without being written.
  • New: an alert when Site Defense’s own uploads rule is removed or edited.
  • Changed: one security email a week by default, instead of an email after every scan. Scan results, waiting updates and lockouts are collected, and anything fixed before Monday is left out. Daily, or straight away as before, can be chosen under Settings, Alerts. A new administrator and Site Defense being switched off are still emailed straight away.
  • Changed: a file that several checks match is listed once in emails and counted as one thing to check.
  • Changed: no new-IP login email while Wordfence is active and already emails every administrator login.
  • New: rate limiting, with separate limits for browsers and bots, and a choice between slowing down and blocking.
  • New: bad bot blocking (site copiers, email harvesters, scraping frameworks, form posts with no browser headers) and optional SEO crawler blocking.
  • New: the fake search engine check uses the crawler IP lists Google, Bing and Apple publish, so it still works when the server’s DNS doesn’t answer.
  • New: your own block list for IP ranges, user agents, referring sites and hostnames, under Settings, Access rules.
  • New: login allowlist for administrators, editors and shop managers, with a wp-config.php escape hatch.
  • New: optional REST API lock for logged-out visitors, with the routes front-end features need left open.
  • New: strong passwords for powerful accounts, and trap usernames can no longer be registered.
  • New: comment spam bot check without a CAPTCHA. On themes and page builders that print their own comment form without WordPress’s hook, it stays out of the way instead of marking real comments as spam.
  • New: more malware signatures from the November cleanup: files that load other files named by the request, uploader backdoors in uploads and mu-plugins, and the watchdog family’s class and author names.
  • New: signatures for 2025 and 2026 WordPress malware campaigns published by GoDaddy, Patchstack and Sansec: DollyWay, the Help TDS fake plugin, the Steam profile injector, the fake WooCommerce security patch, the Gravity Forms, EssentialPlugin, Smart Slider 3 Pro and OptinMonster supply-chain backdoors, WP Smart Thumbnails, the stolen UpdraftCentral key backdoors, the FunnelKit checkout skimmer and the SocGholish loader. Their files, settings, scheduled tasks, admin names and domains are reported.
  • New: two-factor login by email code, for people without an authenticator app. Codes work once, for ten minutes, with a “send a new code” link and backup codes.
  • New: file permissions check on the Hardening tab, with a one-click fix that only takes away write access for others.
  • Changed: requests the site makes to itself (cron, Site Health, plugins fetching their own pages) are never blocked, whatever name they send.
  • Fixed: “not from WordPress.org” findings had an Update button with nothing to update. It is now “Go to Plugins”.
  • Scan emails no longer repeat a file they already told you about when a second check finds it too.

1.1.1

  • Calmer scan emails. A scan only emails findings it hasn’t emailed before, so the same list never arrives twice.
  • Scans you start yourself (button or WP-CLI) no longer send an email: you are already looking at the results.
  • Updates waiting, known vulnerabilities and closed plugins are emailed as “things to do, no sign of a hack”, apart from findings that could point to a break-in.
  • No more “Critical” and “High” labels in emails, and plainer wording in the alerts.

1.1.0

  • New: alert emails are sent as clean HTML in the plugin’s own style (a plain-text copy is included), with the details in a table and a button to the right screen. White-labelled sites show their own name.
  • New: fake search engine blocking. Bots calling themselves Googlebot, Bingbot, Applebot, YandexBot or Baiduspider are checked with reverse and forward DNS.
  • New: 404 probing protection. IPs hunting for missing plugins, backups and shells are blocked.
  • New: optional AI training crawler blocking through robots.txt and the firewall, and a list of the AI bots that visit on the Firewall tab.
  • New: email when updates are waiting, and an optional email for login lockouts (at most one an hour).
  • Fixed: official old jQuery files (1.0.4 to 1.2.6, packed) were reported as “Packed JavaScript, common in injected code”. They now show as a low-priority note that the file is jQuery’s own and out of date.
  • Clearer wording for other packed JavaScript findings.

1.0.0

  • First release.
